newsitem.title: USA: Reader's Digest boss leaves amid condensed earnings.
newsitem.headline: Reader's Digest boss leaves amid condensed earnings.

text.p: One month after slashing its dividend and earnings forecast, publisher Reader's Digest Association Inc. said Monday its chairman and chief executive officer, James Schadt, had resigned.

The company, renowned for its condensed-version books and monthly magazine, said Schadt resigned to pursue personal interests. A company spokeswoman declined to say whether the board asked him to resign.

Former Chief Executive Officer and Chairman George Grune, who is 68, will act as chairman and CEO, effective immediately, while a committee comprised of independent directors searches for a permanent successor to Schadt, 59.
Grune led Reader's Digest's move from a private to a publicly held company. Reader's Digest said its revenues doubled and operating profit increased ninefold during his decade at the helm.
Schadt's departure comes as Reader's Digest faces increasing pressure from investors unhappy with the company's sagging stock price and steadily declining profits, analysts said.
The company's stock has lost more than a third of its value since the start of the year, tumbling from around $40 in January to the mid-20s in recent months.
Wall Street greeted the news of Schadt's resignation with enthusiasm, sending the stock up $2.94 to $27.81 in consolidated afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.

The board was "facing a loss of confidence within the analyst community," said Linda Bannister, an analyst at brokerage Edwards Jones. "Maybe this was a move to get someone in with a different background, with new ideas."

In April, Reader's Digest reported its earnings fell 31 percent to $37.6 million, or 35 cents a share, in the third quarter ending March 31. At that time, the company announced a four-year $400 million programme to aggressively promote its products.

Last month, the company cut its quarterly dividend in half and warned that inventory writedowns and the plan to rejuvenate its business would diminish fiscal fourth-quarter earnings by about 45 cents a share.
Analysts said the company's troubles stem in large part from declining revenues from sales of books and home entertainment, such as video.

"It's really the most profitable piece of the business," said Karen Ficker, an analyst with investment bank Furman Selz. "Although the magazine is the best known piece, it's just the front door of the company."
To get back on track, analysts said the company would need to boost revenues and increase the number of subscribers.
But they agreed that Reader's Digest still benefits from a strong brand name.

Reader's Digest, based in Pleasantville, N.Y., said the board committee that will seek out Schadt's replacement will be led by James Preston, chairman Avon Products Inc. Schadt was not available for comment, and Grune declined to comment.
